pamphlet_excerpts: Wrist Protection: Rigid splints inside wrist guards disperse impact forces away from delicate carpal bones.
Helmet Standards: Multi-impact certified helmets shield the cranial vault during backward falls onto hard surfaces.
Hypothermia Prevention: Synthetic wicking base layers prevent rapid core cooling by transporting sweat from skin.
Laceration Defense: Cut-resistant Kevlar socks guard Achilles tendons against sharp skate blades during collisions.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Surface Evaluation: Examine the rink or pavement for cracks, pooled water, debris, and oil slicks.
Step 2 - Equipment Fitting: Fasten safety pads securely to prevent slippage during sudden falls on hard surfaces.
Step 3 - Fall Execution: Bend knees deeply and drop forward onto knee pads and forearm guards smoothly.
Step 4 - Injury Assessment: Check an injured skater for airway stability, profuse bleeding, and extremity fractures immediately.

quiz_item.question: While skating on an outdoor winter pond, a skater breaks through thin ice into frigid water 30 feet from shore. How should your patrol respond safely?
options: A. Skate out to the edge of the ice hole in a group to pull the skater up by both hands.
B. Stay off the thin ice, call for emergency help, lie flat near shore to spread weight.
C. Instruct the skater to remove their skates and winter jacket in the water before trying to climb out.
D. Have one Scout walk upright to the rim of the broken ice hole carrying a heavy wooden bench.

misconception_pool.misconception: Beginners often believe that extending straight arms during a fall protects the body from injury.
misconception_pool.fact: Bracing with outstretched locked arms transfers impact energy to the wrists, causing radial fractures.

misconception_pool.misconception: Rubbing frostbitten skin vigorously with hands or snow restores blood circulation safely to frozen toes.
misconception_pool.fact: Friction shatters ice crystals inside frozen cells and destroys tissue; warm frostbite gently in 99 to 102 degree F water.

misconception_pool.misconception: Wearing two pairs of thick cotton socks inside skates prevents heel blisters and keeps feet warmer on ice.
misconception_pool.fact: Doubled cotton socks trap moisture, bunch up, and create friction blisters; wear one snug pair of moisture-wicking socks.

misconception_pool.misconception: Bracing a forward fall with outstretched bare hands protects the skater from serious upper-body injury.
misconception_pool.fact: Catching full body weight on stiff, unguarded hands frequently fractures the wrist; wear rigid wrist guards when roller or inline skating.

misconception_pool.misconception: Popping a friction blister on the heel with an unsterilized pin lets a skater return to the rink safely.
misconception_pool.fact: Intact skin acts as a sterile barrier against bacteria; cover small blisters with a moleskin doughnut pad instead of puncturing them.

requirements.lead_text: Working under the supervision of an experienced adult, do ONE of the following options:
requirements.req_text: Working under the supervision of an experienced adult, do ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Ice Skating. Do ALL of the following: (1) Explain the general safety and courtesy guidelines for ice skating. (2) Discuss preparations that must be taken when skating outdoors on natural ice. Explain how to make an ice rescue. (3) Discuss the parts and functions of the different types of ice skates. (4) Describe the proper way to carry ice skates at the rink and for travel. (5) Describe how to store ice skates for long periods of time, such as seasonal storage. (6) Skate forward at least 40 feet and come to a complete stop. Use either a two-foot snowplow stop or a one-foot snowplow stop. (7) After skating forward, glide forward on two feet, then on one foot, first right and then left. (8) Starting from a T position, stroke forward around the test area, avoiding the use of toe picks if wearing figure skates. (9) Glide backward on two feet for at least two times the skater's height. (10) Skate backward for at least 20 feet on two skates. (11) After gaining forward speed, glide forward on two feet, making a turn of 180 degrees around a cone, first to the right and then to the left. (12) Perform forward crossovers in a figure-eight pattern. (13) Explain to your counselor the safety considerations for participating in an ice-skating race. (14) Perform a hockey stop. (b) Option B, Roller Skating. Do ALL of the following: (1) Explain the general safety rules and etiquette guidelines for roller skating. (2) Discuss the parts of a roller skate and their functions. (3) Describe five essential steps to good roller skate care. (4) Skate forward with smooth, linked strokes on two feet for at least 100 feet in both directions around the rink and demonstrate proper techniques for stopping. (5) Skate forward and glide at least 15 feet on one skate, then on the other skate. (6) Perform a forward crossover. (7) Skate backward for at least 40 feet on two skates, then for at least 15 feet on one skate. (8) Skate forward in a slalom pattern for at least 40 feet on two skates, then for at least 20 feet on one skate. (9) Skate backward in a slalom pattern for at least 15 feet on two skates. (10) Shuttle skate once around the rink, bending twice along the way, without stopping. (11) Perform a series of two consecutive spins on skates, OR hop, skip, and jump on skates for at least 10 feet. (12) Perform a stepover. (13) While skating, dribble a basketball at least 40 feet, then back to your starting position, OR push a hockey ball with a stick at least 40 feet, then back to your starting position. (c) Option C, In-Line Skating. Do ALL of the following: (1) Explain the general safety rules and courtesy guidelines for in-line skating. (2) Describe the parts of an in-line skate and their functions. (3) Describe the required and recommended safety equipment for in-line skating. (4) Explain four essential steps to good in-line skate care. (5) Skate forward with smooth, linked strokes on two feet for at least 100 feet. (6) Skate forward and glide at least 15 feet on one skate, then on the other skate. (7) Stop on command on flat pavement using the heel brake. (8) Perform a forward crossover. (9) Perform a series of forward, linked swizzles for at least 40 feet. (10) Skate backward for at least 40 feet in a series of linked, backward swizzles. (11) From a strong pace, perform a lunge turn around an object predetermined by your counselor. (12) Perform a mohawk. (13) Perform a series of at least four one-footed downhill slaloms on pavement with a gentle slope. (14) Describe how to pass a pedestrian or another skater from behind. (15) Describe at least three ways to avoid an unforeseen obstacle while skating. (16) Describe two ways to get on and off a curb, and demonstrate at least one of these methods. (d) Option D, Skateboarding. Do ALL of the following: (1) Explain the history and evolution of skateboarding. (2) Describe the benefits of skateboarding (physical fitness, balance, coordination, perseverance, and creativity). (3) Explain the safety rules and courtesy guidelines for skateboarding, including right-of-way and communication signals and warnings. (4) Explain the protective gear needed to skate safely, including helmet, knee pads, elbow pads, and wrist guards, and show how to wear them correctly. (5) Describe the two main styles of skateboarding (street and vert), and describe common skatepark features (ramps, manual pad, rails, spine, etc.). (6) Explain skateboard anatomy (deck, trucks, wheels, hardware, etc.). (7) Build a board by assembling all pieces (deck, wheels, trucks, hardware, and grip tape) in the proper order. (8) Explain skateboard maintenance (cleaning, adjusting bolts, and replacing parts). (9) Explain the difference between regular and goofy stance, and demonstrate your preferred stance. (10) Demonstrate how to push, cruise, and carve on flat ground. (11) Show at least two braking and stopping techniques. (12) Do a basic ollie and at least one variation. (13) Show how to drop-in from coping. (14) Demonstrate THREE skateboarding tricks from the following types: (a) Flat ground tricks (b) Flip and shove-it tricks (c) Grind and slide tricks (d) Air and grab tricks (e) Footplant tricks

(2) Discuss preparations that must be taken when skating outdoors on natural ice. Explain how to make an ice rescue. (3) Discuss the parts and functions of the different types of ice skates. (4) Describe the proper way to carry ice skates at the rink and for travel. (5) Describe how to store ice skates for long periods of time, such as seasonal storage. (8) Starting from a T position, stroke forward around the test area, avoiding the use of toe picks if wearing figure skates. (9) Glide backward on two feet for at least two times the skater's height. (10) Skate backward for at least 20 feet on two skates. (11) After gaining forward speed, glide forward on two feet, making a turn of 180 degrees around a cone, first to the right and then to the left. (12) Perform forward crossovers in a figure-eight pattern. (13) Explain to your counselor the safety considerations for participating in an ice-skating race. (14) Perform a hockey stop.

(5) Skate forward and glide at least 15 feet on one skate, then on the other skate. (6) Perform a forward crossover. (8) Skate forward in a slalom pattern for at least 40 feet on two skates, then for at least 20 feet on one skate. (9) Skate backward in a slalom pattern for at least 15 feet on two skates. (11) Perform a series of two consecutive spins on skates, OR hop, skip, and jump on skates for at least 10 feet. (12) Perform a stepover. sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option C, In-Line Skating. Do ALL of the following: (1) Explain the general safety rules and courtesy guidelines for in-line skating. (2) Describe the parts of an in-line skate and their functions. (3) Describe the required and recommended safety equipment for in-line skating. (4) Explain four essential steps to good in-line skate care. (5) Skate forward with smooth, linked strokes on two feet for at least 100 feet. (6) Skate forward and glide at least 15 feet on one skate, then on the other skate. (7) Stop on command on flat pavement using the heel brake. (8) Perform a forward crossover. (9) Perform a series of forward, linked swizzles for at least 40 feet. (10) Skate backward for at least 40 feet in a series of linked, backward swizzles. (11) From a strong pace, perform a lunge turn around an object predetermined by your counselor. (12) Perform a mohawk. (13) Perform a series of at least four one-footed downhill slaloms on pavement with a gentle slope. (14) Describe how to pass a pedestrian or another skater from behind. (15) Describe at least three ways to avoid an unforeseen obstacle while skating. (16) Describe two ways to get on and off a curb, and demonstrate at least one of these methods.

sub_requirements.text: Option D, Skateboarding. Do ALL of the following: (1) Explain the history and evolution of skateboarding. (2) Describe the benefits of skateboarding (physical fitness, balance, coordination, perseverance, and creativity). (3) Explain the safety rules and courtesy guidelines for skateboarding, including right-of-way and communication signals and warnings. (4) Explain the protective gear needed to skate safely, including helmet, knee pads, elbow pads, and wrist guards, and show how to wear them correctly. (5) Describe the two main styles of skateboarding (street and vert), and describe common skatepark features (ramps, manual pad, rails, spine, etc.). (6) Explain skateboard anatomy (deck, trucks, wheels, hardware, etc.). (7) Build a board by assembling all pieces (deck, wheels, trucks, hardware, and grip tape) in the proper order. (8) Explain skateboard maintenance (cleaning, adjusting bolts, and replacing parts). (9) Explain the difference between regular and goofy stance, and demonstrate your preferred stance. (10) Demonstrate how to push, cruise, and carve on flat ground. (11) Show at least two braking and stopping techniques. (12) Do a basic ollie and at least one variation. (13) Show how to drop-in from coping. (14) Demonstrate THREE skateboarding tricks from the following types: (a) Flat ground tricks (b) Flip and shove-it tricks (c) Grind and slide tricks (d) Air and grab tricks (e) Footplant tricks.

requirements.description: Working under the supervision of an experienced adult, do ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Ice Skating. Do ALL of the following: (1) Explain the general safety and courtesy guidelines for ice skating. (2) Discuss preparations that must be taken when skating outdoors on natural ice. Explain how to make an ice rescue. (3) Discuss the parts and functions of the different types of ice skates. (4) Describe the proper way to carry ice skates at the rink and for travel. (5) Describe how to store ice skates for long periods of time, such as seasonal storage. (6) Skate forward at least 40 feet and come to a complete stop. Use either a two-foot snowplow stop or a one-foot snowplow stop. (7) After skating forward, glide forward on two feet, then on one foot, first right and then left. (8) Starting from a T position, stroke forward around the test area, avoiding the use of toe picks if wearing figure skates. (9) Glide backward on two feet for at least two times the skater's height. (10) Skate backward for at least 20 feet on two skates. (11) After gaining forward speed, glide forward on two feet, making a turn of 180 degrees around a cone, first to the right and then to the left. (12) Perform forward crossovers in a figure-eight pattern. (13) Explain to your counselor the safety considerations for participating in an ice-skating race. (14) Perform a hockey stop. (b) Option B, Roller Skating. Do ALL of the following: (1) Explain the general safety rules and etiquette guidelines for roller skating. (2) Discuss the parts of a roller skate and their functions. (3) Describe five essential steps to good roller skate care. (4) Skate forward with smooth, linked strokes on two feet for at least 100 feet in both directions around the rink and demonstrate proper techniques for stopping. (5) Skate forward and glide at least 15 feet on one skate, then on the other skate. (6) Perform a forward crossover. (7) Skate backward for at least 40 feet on two skates, then for at least 15 feet on one skate. (8) Skate forward in a slalom pattern for at least 40 feet on two skates, then for at least 20 feet on one skate. (9) Skate backward in a slalom pattern for at least 15 feet on two skates. (10) Shuttle skate once around the rink, bending twice along the way, without stopping. (11) Perform a series of two consecutive spins on skates, OR hop, skip, and jump on skates for at least 10 feet. (12) Perform a stepover. (13) While skating, dribble a basketball at least 40 feet, then back to your starting position, OR push a hockey ball with a stick at least 40 feet, then back to your starting position. (c) Option C, In-Line Skating. Do ALL of the following: (1) Explain the general safety rules and courtesy guidelines for in-line skating. (2) Describe the parts of an in-line skate and their functions. (3) Describe the required and recommended safety equipment for in-line skating. (4) Explain four essential steps to good in-line skate care. (5) Skate forward with smooth, linked strokes on two feet for at least 100 feet. (6) Skate forward and glide at least 15 feet on one skate, then on the other skate. (7) Stop on command on flat pavement using the heel brake. (8) Perform a forward crossover. (9) Perform a series of forward, linked swizzles for at least 40 feet. (10) Skate backward for at least 40 feet in a series of linked, backward swizzles. (11) From a strong pace, perform a lunge turn around an object predetermined by your counselor. (12) Perform a mohawk. (13) Perform a series of at least four one-footed downhill slaloms on pavement with a gentle slope. (14) Describe how to pass a pedestrian or another skater from behind. (15) Describe at least three ways to avoid an unforeseen obstacle while skating. (16) Describe two ways to get on and off a curb, and demonstrate at least one of these methods. (d) Option D, Skateboarding. Do ALL of the following: (1) Explain the history and evolution of skateboarding. (2) Describe the benefits of skateboarding (physical fitness, balance, coordination, perseverance, and creativity). (3) Explain the safety rules and courtesy guidelines for skateboarding, including right-of-way and communication signals and warnings. (4) Explain the protective gear needed to skate safely, including helmet, knee pads, elbow pads, and wrist guards, and show how to wear them correctly. (5) Describe the two main styles of skateboarding (street and vert), and describe common skatepark features (ramps, manual pad, rails, spine, etc.). (6) Explain skateboard anatomy (deck, trucks, wheels, hardware, etc.). (7) Build a board by assembling all pieces (deck, wheels, trucks, hardware, and grip tape) in the proper order. (8) Explain skateboard maintenance (cleaning, adjusting bolts, and replacing parts). (9) Explain the difference between regular and goofy stance, and demonstrate your preferred stance. (10) Demonstrate how to push, cruise, and carve on flat ground. (11) Show at least two braking and stopping techniques. (12) Do a basic ollie and at least one variation. (13) Show how to drop-in from coping. (14) Demonstrate THREE skateboarding tricks from the following types: (a) Flat ground tricks (b) Flip and shove-it tricks (c) Grind and slide tricks (d) Air and grab tricks (e) Footplant tricks

misconception_pool.misconception: Novice skaters assume stiff legs and an upright spine provide the most stable skating posture.
misconception_pool.fact: Flexed knees and ankles lower the skater center of gravity, maintaining balance through irregular surface changes.

misconception_pool.misconception: Milky white snow ice has the same load-bearing strength as clear blue lake ice of equal thickness.
misconception_pool.fact: White snow ice contains trapped air pockets and has only about half the strength of clear new ice, requiring double the thickness.

misconception_pool.misconception: Storing wet ice skates inside plush fabric soakers or a closed gym bag prevents blade rust overnight.
misconception_pool.fact: Moisture trapped against steel blades causes rapid rusting and pitting; wipe blades completely dry with a cloth before storing them.

misconception_pool.misconception: Walking upright out onto the edge of an ice hole is the fastest way to pull a fallen skater out of freezing water.
misconception_pool.fact: Standing near thin ice concentrates weight and breaks the edge; rescuers must stay on shore or lie flat to distribute weight with a pole.

misconception_pool.misconception: Pushing straight backward with a flat skate blade or wheel generates forward propulsion on a skating rink.
misconception_pool.fact: Flat blades simply slide backward without grip; skaters must push outward at an angle against the inside edge to generate forward thrust.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: While skating on an outdoor winter pond, a skater breaks through thin ice into frigid water 30 feet from shore. How should your patrol respond safely?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: While skating on an outdoor winter pond, a skater breaks through thin ice into frigid water 30 feet from shore. How should your patrol respond safely?
options: A. Skate out to the edge of the ice hole in a group to pull the skater up by both hands.
B. Stay off the thin ice, call for emergency help, lie flat near shore to spread weight.
C. Instruct the skater to remove their skates and winter jacket in the water before trying to climb out.
D. Have one Scout walk upright to the rim of the broken ice hole carrying a heavy wooden bench.
choices: A. Skate out to the edge of the ice hole in a group to pull the skater up by both hands.
B. Stay off the thin ice, call for emergency help, lie flat near shore to spread weight.
C. Instruct the skater to remove their skates and winter jacket in the water before trying to climb out.
D. Have one Scout walk upright to the rim of the broken ice hole carrying a heavy wooden bench.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Stay off the thin ice, call for emergency help, lie flat near shore to spread weight, and extend a long reach/throw aid (branch, hockey stick, or rope) while coaching the skater to kick horizontally onto firm ice and roll away from the hole.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Walking or skating up to an ice breakthrough hole causes the ice edge to collapse under rescuers; follow Reach-Throw protocol and keep clothing/skates on for buoyancy and traction.

patrol_quiz_bank.question: Which safety rule applies specifically to preparing for outdoor ice skating on a frozen pond, lake, or river?
options: A. A thin layer of overnight frost on a pond guarantees safe skating across the entire surface
B. Ice is always thickest directly underneath low bridges and where streams flow into a lake
C. Natural ice must be verified for safe thickness, and skaters should never skate alone on frozen water bodies
D. Driving a heavy vehicle onto the pond is the safest way for Scouts to test unknown ice thickness
choices: A. A thin layer of overnight frost on a pond guarantees safe skating across the entire surface
B. Ice is always thickest directly underneath low bridges and where streams flow into a lake
C. Natural ice must be verified for safe thickness, and skaters should never skate alone on frozen water bodies
D. Driving a heavy vehicle onto the pond is the safest way for Scouts to test unknown ice thickness
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Natural ice must be verified for safe thickness, and skaters should never skate alone on frozen water bodies
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Before skating on natural outdoor ice, you must verify that the ice thickness is checked and approved by local authorities, never skate alone, and stay clear of thin ice near inflows, bridges, or dark snow-covered patches (p. 49).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: After finishing an ice skating session, you remove your skates at the rink bench. What must you do to the steel blades before placing your skates inside hard plastic walk-guards or a carry bag?
options: Leave a thin coat of melted ice on the blades so they cool evenly
Wipe the blades completely dry with a soft towel and store them in breathable terry-cloth soakers (never leave wet blades sealed inside hard rubber/plastic guards)
Scrape the hollow edge against concrete to remove ice crystals
Pack snow around the boot leather to preserve its stiffness
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: Option B - Wipe the blades completely dry with a soft towel and store them in breathable terry-cloth soakers (never leave wet blades sealed inside hard rubber/plastic guards)
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Hard plastic guards are only for walking off the ice; storing wet blades inside non-breathable guards traps moisture and rapidly rusts the sharpened hollow edges.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: While in-line skating on a shared multi-use path, you approach a slower pedestrian from behind. What is the proper passing etiquette and safety procedure?
options: Weave closely past their right shoulder at full speed without speaking
Slow down to a controlled speed, call out 'Passing on your left!' well in advance, and pass with generous clearance on the left
Grab onto their backpack to match their walking pace
Jump over the curb into oncoming street traffic without looking
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: Option B - Slow down to a controlled speed, call out 'Passing on your left!' well in advance, and pass with generous clearance on the left
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: In-line skaters must yield to pedestrians, control speed, give an audible warning ('Passing on your left!'), and pass at a safe distance.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Before dropping in or skating at a public skatepark (Option D - Skateboarding), what personal protective equipment and pre-ride inspection are required?
options: Only a baseball cap and loose-laced canvas shoes
A properly fitted ASTM/CPSC skateboard helmet, wrist guards, knee pads, and elbow pads, plus checking truck kingpins, axle nuts, wheels, and deck grip tape
Removing the front truck bolts so the board turns sharper on ramps
Oiling the wheel bearings with cooking oil immediately before riding wet concrete
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: Option B - A properly fitted ASTM/CPSC skateboard helmet, wrist guards, knee pads, and elbow pads, plus checking truck kingpins, axle nuts, wheels, and deck grip tape
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Scouting America skateboarding safety requires a certified helmet, wrist guards, knee pads, and elbow pads, along with inspecting trucks, wheels, bearings, and grip tape before every session.
